metric_rationale: In this experimental design, the trials can be divided into 'compensatory' (where the single best cue points to one option, but the sum of the remaining cues points to the other) and 'non-compensatory' (where the best cue and the sum of cues agree). This metric computes the difference in the rate of Take-The-Best (TTB) consistent choices between non-compensatory and compensatory trials. For the TTB model, this difference will be near zero because it uses the same one-reason strategy on both trial types. For the Weighted Additive (WADD) model, the difference will be significantly greater than zero because it frequently chooses the opposite of TTB on compensatory trials while agreeing with TTB on non-compensatory trials.

The experimental design is carefully constructed such that for every trial, the single most valid discriminating cue predicts one option (which Take The Best will choose), while the sum of the remaining discriminating cues predicts the other option (which Weighted Additive will choose). By measuring the proportion of trials where the subject's response aligns with the TTB prediction, we obtain a metric that will be very high (~1.0) under TTB and very low (~0.0) under WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices favoring the Tallying model's prediction on the critical dissociation trials (Trials 1 and 2). In these trials, one option is endorsed by the two most valid cues (sum of validities = 1.80) and the other by the three least valid cues (sum of validities = 1.65). Tallying simply counts the features and robustly prefers the option with three positive features. WADD, evaluating the weighted validities, will typically favor the option with the two highly valid features. The metric will return values close to 1.0 for data simulated under Tallying, and substantially lower values (often below 0.5) for data simulated under WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of WADD-compliant choices on the critical dissociation trials (Trials 1 and 7). On these trials, one option has two high-validity features ([1, 1, 0, 0, 0]) while the other has three low-validity features ([0, 0, 1, 1, 1]). The Weighted Additive (WADD) model strongly prefers the former, whereas the Tallying (Equal Weight) model strictly prefers the latter because it counts more positive features. The metric will yield a high value for WADD and a low value for Tallying, perfectly discriminating the two models.

Pure Tallying strictly counts the total number of positive features. On trials where both options have the exact same number of positive features (Trials 2 and 4), Tallying is completely indifferent and will choose either option with 50% probability, regardless of the subject's noise parameters. Thresholded Tallying, however, applies a soft filter that down-weights lower-validity features. Even when its threshold is low and it mimics Tallying, the logistic filter strictly preserves the order of validities, meaning it will always assign a higher score to the option with more high-validity features. By measuring the proportion of choices for the option with more high-validity features specifically on trials where the total feature counts are tied, we isolate a condition where Tallying predicts exactly 0.5 (with minimal variance) while Thresholded Tallying predicts a value strictly greater than 0.5.

For the Pure Tallying model, options A and B in the tie trials (trials 5, 6, 7, and 9) have the exact same unweighted sum of features. Consequently, Pure Tallying predicts a choice probability of exactly 0.5 for Option A on every single one of these trials, regardless of the subject's noise (beta) or lapse (epsilon) parameters. The variance of this metric for Pure Tallying subjects will be extremely low, driven purely by binomial sampling noise over the 36 tie trials per subject. Conversely, Thresholded Tallying softly filters out the low-validity features. Because Option A is heavily loaded with high-validity features in all these tie trials, Thresholded Tallying will strongly prefer Option A whenever its threshold parameter is sufficiently high to engage the filtering. This creates a large, directional mean shift for Thresholded Tallying (> 0.5) against a mathematically locked baseline (0.5) with minimal variance for Pure Tallying, guaranteeing a highly significant t-statistic.
